panels.title: Files Discovered (total)
panels.description: A 0 means no work was recorded in this window. To tell idle from stuck, read it against the backlog rows: pending messages with a 0 total is the stale-connector signature. Total for the dashboard time range, not a rate. A scale-to-zero connector often finishes its work inside a single scrape interval, so the counter is born at its final value and rate() / increase() are exactly 0 - measured in dev: an 8-file scan took ~7ms and every sample of the counter read 8, so every rate panel showed 0.00 and the percentiles went blank. max_over_time recovers the final value per series precisely because the counter dies with the pod; summing across pods gives the work actually done in the window. Read this row first when the pod is asleep, and the rate panels below when it is under load.

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(cifs_scanner_files_discovered_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) - (sum(max_over_time(cifs_scanner_items_sent_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}[$__range])) or vector(0))

panels.title: Unit Cost — seconds per file, by stage
Cost per File Discovered
panels.description: Seconds of directory-processing work per file discovered, over the dashboard range. The predictive number for the discovery stage: at 184us/file measured in dev on 2026-09-03, a 10M-file share costs roughly 31 minutes of directory work. TWO CAVEATS. (1) It includes the root directory's fan-out - one NATS publish per subdirectory - which is a per-DIRECTORY cost amortised over files. In the dev run the root alone took ~8s of the 18.42s total, so it nearly doubles the figure; without it the cost is ~104us/file. The prediction therefore holds only for shares of similar shape: the same file count spread over 10x the directories costs more per file. (2) files_discovered_total carries no datasource_id label while the histogram does, so with two datasources scanning concurrently the denominator mixes them while the numerator does not. Correct for one scan at a time.

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(cifs_scanner_scan_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(cifs_scanner_files_discovered_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1)

panels.title: ACL Cost per Item Augmented
panels.description: Seconds of ACL query time per item the augmenter touched. This is the ACL SLICE ONLY, not the full cost of augmenting an item: profiling in dev put ACL at ~41% of processItem, statx at ~36% and URN resolve at ~19%, so the true per-item cost is roughly 2.4x this number. It is still the single dominant component and the one that drives KEDA to scale the augment stage to several pods. No histogram covers the whole per-item path today. augment.go:204 already computes a whole-batch duration but only writes it to a log line, and batch wall-clock would conflate internal worker concurrency anyway - the honest fix would be a processItem histogram. Compare against Cost per File Discovered to the left: that gap is why augment saturates and discovery does not.

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(cifs_augmenter_acl_query_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(cifs_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1)

panels.title: Cost per Content Fetch
panels.description: Mean seconds per content fetch over the dashboard range, computed from the histogram's own _sum and _count so it does not depend on bucket boundaries at all. Unlike the two panels to its left this one has a matching denominator - both halves come from the same histogram - so no label mismatch is possible and no datasource caveat applies. Content fetch cost scales with file SIZE, not file count, so read it together with Upload Throughput rather than on its own: a rising cost per fetch with flat throughput means the share got slower, while a rising cost with rising throughput just means bigger files.

targets.expr: (sum(max_over_time(cifs_content_fetch_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(cifs_content_fetch_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1)

panels.title: Dir Processing p95
panels.description: Wall-clock of processing ONE directory end to end: listing entries, statx of every file, ACL query when enabled, and publishing the items (cifsscan.go:655-687). NOT the job duration - the traversal forks one NATS message per subdirectory, so a scan of 2009 directories produces 2009 independent observations and none of them spans the whole job. No connector-side metric can measure the job: nobody owns it end to end. Aggregated with max_over_time over the dashboard range instead of rate(): a scale-to-zero pod often finishes inside one 30s scrape interval, leaving a single sample that rate() cannot derive a slope from - measured in dev on 2026-09-03, this panel was blank four minutes after a 100k scan. GUARDRAIL: if the mean (_sum/_count) reads BELOW the p50, the buckets have lost resolution and the percentiles are interpolation artifacts rather than measurements. That happened here with buckets starting at 0.1s measuring 5ms latencies: histogram_quantile returned 0.1 x q for every quantile.

panels.title: Scanner Throughput (rate, 5m)
panels.description: discovered = files that reached processing; sent = items handed to the batch sender. files_processed_total and items_sent_total are incremented on adjacent lines in the same else-branch (cifsscan.go), so they are identical by construction and the real funnel is discovered to sent. Neither counter carries datasource_id, so a loss cannot yet be attributed to a share.

panels.title: NATS — Scanner Backlog
panels.description: Messages waiting on the scanner durable - the answer to "how backed up is it". Scanner and augmenter run in the same deployment and share this one durable (cifs-scanner-v1): handleCifsForkJE and handleItemBatchJE are dispatched by message type off a single consumer. num_pending therefore blends CIFSFork and ItemBatch work, so augmenter backlog is not separable here and KEDA cannot tell them apart either. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter (no namespace/pod labels).

panels.title: NATS — In Flight (unacked)
panels.description: Delivered but not yet acked: work currently inside the pods. Also the signal KEDA's ack-capacity trigger scales on. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter (no namespace/pod labels).

panels.title: NATS — Redelivered
panels.description: Messages redelivered after an ack timeout. Sustained growth with a flat items_sent rate is the stalled-connector signature. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter (no namespace/pod labels).

panels.title: Replicas
panels.description: Current replicas of the scanner deployment, from the HPA KEDA manages. minReplicaCount is 0, so 0 replicas with an empty queue is normal.

panels.title: Max Replicas
panels.description: Ceiling from the ScaledObject. Replicas pinned here while the backlog grows means the connector is capped, not idle.

panels.title: NATS — Backlog Slope (2m)
panels.description: Per-second growth of the backlog, clamped at 0. Verbatim the query KEDA's trend-based trigger evaluates; above 0.5 it asks for more pods.

panels.title: NATS — Scanner Consumer Backlog
panels.description: Backlog on JE_CIFS/cifs-scanner-v1. Pending high while items_sent is flat means the connector is not draining. Scanner and augmenter run in the same deployment and share this one durable (cifs-scanner-v1): handleCifsForkJE and handleItemBatchJE are dispatched by message type off a single consumer. num_pending therefore blends CIFSFork and ItemBatch work, so augmenter backlog is not separable here and KEDA cannot tell them apart either. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter (no namespace/pod labels).

panels.title: KEDA — Replicas: current vs desired vs max
panels.description: current below desired means scaling is in progress or blocked; current pinned at max means capped. Scale-down is deliberately slow (cooldown 900s, 600s stabilization window), so a flat line for ten minutes after a burst is configuration, not a stuck HPA.

panels.title: KEDA — ack-capacity signal vs threshold
panels.description: KEDA's ack-capacity trigger: replicas = ceil(ack_pending / 1000). The red line is that threshold; crossing it is what asks for another pod.

panels.title: KEDA — trend-based signal vs threshold
panels.description: KEDA's trend-based trigger: slope of the backlog over 2m, clamped at 0 so only growth counts. Threshold 0.5, activation 0.1. The pipeline-full trigger is not rendered in dev (capacity is unset), so this plus ack-capacity and pending-wakeup is the whole scaling story.

panels.title: Augmenter Items by Outcome (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Terminal outcome per item the augmenter touched. The augmenter has no autoscaling of its own - it shares the scanner's deployment and durable, so its capacity and backlog are the scanner panels above. outcome="missing" is also counted by items_skipped_not_found_total; both are incremented for the same event on adjacent lines, so never sum the two.

panels.title: Augmenter ACL Query Duration — p50 / p95 / p99
Pods Up
panels.description: Content pods scale 0↔N with KEDA — 0 pods with an empty queue is normal.

panels.title: Errors (5m)
panels.description: Number of content fetch requests that failed in the last 5 minutes. Counter increase on cifs_content_fetch_total{success="false"}.

panels.title: Upload Throughput
panels.description: Bytes per second confirmed by the content transfer service (rate over cifs_content_uploaded_bytes_total).

panels.title: Mount Acquire p95 (5m)
panels.description: p95 of successful mount acquires on the content pod. Failed acquires are tracked separately (cifs_content_mount_acquire_failure_duration_seconds).

panels.title: Content Fetches by error_code (rate, 5m)
panels.description: error_code="NONE" is the success path; NAK_* codes are infra-level failures.

panels.title: Content Requests In-Flight
panels.description: Requests currently inside the handler — content-mode saturation signal (the counterpart of the scanner's worker_busy). Authoritative backlog (num_pending) lives on the NATS server.

panels.title: NATS — Content Consumer Redelivery
panels.description: nats_consumer_num_redelivered for the content durable (content-fetch-cifs). Rising = fetch requests failing and being retried; sustained growth toward MaxDeliver=3 means messages are about to be dropped as poison. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter (no namespace/pod labels).

panels.title: KEDA — Content Replicas: current vs desired vs max
panels.description: The content deployment scales independently of the scanner, off its own ScaledObject watching CONTENT_FETCH/content-fetch-cifs.

panels.title: KEDA — Content Trigger Signals
panels.description: Signals behind the content ScaledObject. The consumer_name regex covers both the batch durable and the interactive one used by See Content, which has its own interactive-wakeup trigger. Server-side signal from the NATS exporter (no namespace/pod labels).

panels.title: Files Gone (5m)
panels.description: Files discovered by an earlier scan that were no longer on the share when the augmenter or the content fetcher went back for them. Caveat on the content series: FETCH_ERROR_NOT_FOUND is emitted from three places and only one is a vanished file - fs.ErrNotExist, an ELOOP on a symlink swapped in mid-open, and the not-a-regular-file rejection in handler.go, which fires for symlinks, devices, pipes and sockets. On a share with symlinks this over-counts. Splitting it needs a connector change (a distinct metric label behind the same wire code).

targets.expr: (sum(increase(cifs_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod", outcome="missing"}[5m])) or vector(0)) + (sum(increase(cifs_content_fetch_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod", error_code="FETCH_ERROR_NOT_FOUND"}[5m])) or vector(0))

panels.title: Files Gone % (augment)
panels.description: Share of augmented items whose file was already gone from the share, over the dashboard time range. The absolute count next to it cannot carry the meaning on its own: 500 gone out of 100k is 0.5 percent normal churn, 500 out of 600 is a mass deletion, a stale index or a mount pointing at the wrong path - same number, opposite conclusion. A file disappearing is not a pipeline failure, it is reality, so read this as 'look at this' rather than 'something is broken'. Augment only: content NOT_FOUND is excluded because it is a different population (content fetches one file per request, so it has no comparable denominator). max_over_time rather than rate for the same reason as the Totals row - the work often finishes inside one scrape interval. clamp_min on the denominator makes an idle window read 0 instead of NaN.

targets.expr: 100 * ((sum(max_over_time(cifs_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod", outcome="missing"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min((sum(max_over_time(cifs_augmenter_items_processed_total{namespace="$namespace", pod=~"$pod"}[$__range])) or vector(0)), 1))

panels.title: Files Gone by stage (rate, 5m)
panels.description: Two series on purpose: a file missing at augment time and one missing at content-fetch time are different moments in the pipeline and are diagnosed differently. Caveat on the content series: FETCH_ERROR_NOT_FOUND is emitted from three places and only one is a vanished file - fs.ErrNotExist, an ELOOP on a symlink swapped in mid-open, and the not-a-regular-file rejection in handler.go, which fires for symlinks, devices, pipes and sockets. On a share with symlinks this over-counts. Splitting it needs a connector change (a distinct metric label behind the same wire code).
